posts.body_html:
DJ-what are your lowest temps that the drosophyllums have experienced and still survived? Lowest I've had Drosophyllums at is 28F, it would be interesting to find out at what temperature/amount of time exposed to freezing temps. will drosophyllum plants bite the dust. It's shocking to see how messed up they look like when completely frozen, only for the plant to look completely normal a few days later once the frost has passed.

In other news, I transplanted a big 3 year old mother plant a week ago and it's growing, so transplanting does work. The roots didn't get too messed up though...I wonder if they can take transplant shock better during the winter when they're growing really slow. Bet that's the case....

The lowest temperature they have experienced here was 20 degrees overnight with warming into the 40s the next day. I don’t know the time period at that low temp though, but guessing maybe 4 or 5 hours at most? They have yet to experience 24/7 freezing temps as it always warms up to above freezing during the day. January is when we usually get 24/7 freezing for brief periods of time, so a chance we will see a limit then. Guess I should start keeping a log.

> In other news, I transplanted a big 3 year old mother plant a week ago and it's growing, so transplanting does work. The roots didn't get too messed up though...I wonder if they can take transplant shock better during the winter when they're growing really slow. Bet that's the case....

Nice! I have not tried transplanting an adult droso myself, but have had good success with seedlings up to 4” or 5” tall. I do suspect transplanting may be easier on them in winter when growth is slowed, but have not done so myself. I had one good-sized seedling whose roots reached to the bottom of a gallon nursery pot that completely collapsed after transplanting, only to sprout back to life a few days later (noticed only when I went to dump the pot). I know now not to give up on transplanted plants too quickly when they look to be deceased, ha.

posts.body_html:
Very nice Jeff, thanks for sharing the link!

DJ: in 4" plastic pots, dozens of plants have been transplanted all year round without any issues, since you can take the whole thing out like a cake and have zero root disturbance.

On the other hand, once you have a big old plant that has outgrown its clay pot, the roots get stuck to the sides and bottom of the pot. When you transplant, some of those roots that are glued to the sides get torn off. In past experiments, breaking these roots caused the drosophyllum plant to slightly wilt, and then die a slow death after struggling for a month. Only difference is that these transplantings were done during the spring when the plants were big and growing fast. With the "dormant" transplant, there was no wilting despite some minimal root damage, and the plant is still in perfect condition as of this morning.

The hypothesis is that best time to transplant is when the plant is in very slow growth, but not under stress. Plants seem to be stressed when:
1) it freezes and thaws
2) it's the middle of summer and it's very hot
3) it just rained and all the dew has been washed off.
4) Plants slightly wilted from lack of water

What I'd like to try out, but lack the cajones to do, is to shave off 20-30% of the root mass of fully mature, adult plants during the slow growth period (maybe 3-4 specimens) and see what happens once transplanted into a bigger pot. This will likely prove or disprove the dormancy hypothesis. I probably lost only 5% of the roots with my recent transplanting experiment, and it's possible that a few plants during the grow season could survive this anyways.

posts.body_html:
That all makes perfect sense for transplanting adults, good information!

As for shaving off 20-30% of the root mass, I know someone who was successful at getting flower stalk cuttings to root by soaking them in GA3. Perhaps this, or a Superthrive soak, would be beneficial to do to the root mass after giving the roots a “haircut”? I would love to test this out myself at some point, biting nails, when I build up enough adult plants again. The two adults I have now are far too stressed this winter so poor candidates. I am hoping to build a proper space next year to over-winter several pots of Drosophyllum protected from freezing.

This one has been outside all winter along with one other (I move them under a table when it rains hard), photo was taken yesterday. This is the same plant as the earlier-posted frosty photo, definitely showing the stress of frequent freeze/thaw cycles. The other one looks much the same. I will be very surprised if they make it to spring, but the knowledge gained hopefully will lessen my sadness/guilt.

posts.body_html:
hunter-that's beautiful, great job!

DJ: Fingers crossed for you, I suspect an early stage of rot is creeping into the stems on that plant. That's exactly what every last one I had that perished looked like a month or two before they bit the dust. One head will get hit, and then slowly they'll all succumb. However, I've had plants that have lost heads yet they still survived....for another 6 months and then croaked, LOL

Got some more updates, but perhaps I'll save most of them for when I get pictures up. Spoiler alert: I got some seeds to germinate in the ground, although it wasn't on purpose! Some of the plants produced so many seeds that they got all over the place.

Haven't taken photos in so long, it's been really busy. It finally stopped raining for a few days here in Northern California, so the dewy pines are starting to get all sticky. I transplanted 2 of the mother plants this winter, and both of them had some level of root damage, but it was minimal. No shock, no wilting, no leaves without sticky mucilage aka no stress occurred. When I have more plants, I will cut up some of the roots to test my "dormancy" hypothesis, but for now, risking a few of the fatties doesn't seem worth it. Photos taken 1/27/15:

this first one is from Cortes De La Frontera, Andalucia, SPAIN. This individual is now 3 years old I think?





Finally! These plants have been devoid of "dew" for more than a month now because of the El Nino rains. A little break from the rain gets them "juiced up" to catch insects:


some seedlings and one old timer in the middle:
